title: Study Abroad Report: Tulane University
paragraphs: For about two months, from the end of March to the end of May 2016, I studied abroad at Tulane University in New Orleans, Louisiana, in the United States. My reasons for choosing this university were a vague longing for American medicine and the aim of improving my English skills. In the pre-departure training I practiced history taking, physical examination and presentations in English. Partly to test the results of that, I went abroad with a mixture of anxiety and expectation about how much medicine I could learn with my own English ability.

For the first two weeks I rotated through cardiology. Since it was the first department I rotated through, I did not know what to do and ran around in confusion. I basically followed a fellow, but at first it was along the lines of "watch from behind," and I just watched them work. Thinking this would not do, I asked questions actively myself, and they taught me very carefully. When I studied in Japan I learned almost entirely passively, so asking questions on my own was hard at first, and I was made to realize how soft I had been until then. However, once I got used to it, I asked about what I did not understand and also actively took patients, and this teaching method seemed efficient and good. During the clerkship I was able to see cases rarely seen in Japan, such as a patient with chest pain due to drugs and a patient who had received a transplant of another organ, which was educational.

For the next two weeks I rotated through neurology. Here for the first time I went around with three students. When a local student takes a patient, before the resident comes they do rounds on their own patient, gather the patient's information accurately, make a solid assessment and discuss with the resident. They could also take the history and perform the physical examination of newly referred patients accurately, and worked properly as doctors. It was impressive that the patients did not have an atmosphere of looking down on them because they were students and treated them as doctors. While actually taking patients and doing history taking, physical examination and presentations, there were scenes in which I felt my advance preparation paid off, but I was often keenly made aware that I was inferior to the local students. I strongly felt that I must work harder, and it became my driving force for studying. During the clerkship I tried to examine as many patients as possible. Examining a patient who complained of weakness in the limbs due to drug abuse is a good memory.

For the last two weeks I rotated through the MICU. The doctors seemed busy and again almost never taught me anything on their own initiative, but by asking questions actively I was able to learn about intensive care, little by little. Since it was my third department, I felt that my questions and discussions had become more fluent than before, and I felt my English ability improving.

During my study abroad I was always thinking about what is different between American and Japanese medicine. Before going, I had thought that the United States provides medical care far superior to Japan's and must be doing things I had never seen. However, although of course I did not visit all American universities, as far as Tulane University is concerned, I felt there was not much difference from the level of Japanese medicine. Yet there were many things that impressed me when I went there. For example, patients' enthusiasm for medical care is different. Local patients could explain their present illness in detail and remembered exactly the drugs they were using and even their doses, and perhaps because they pay more for medical care than in Japan, they seemed highly interested in it. The difference in the education system was also impressive. The local students worked just like residents and tried to learn actively on their own, and seeing this I was again made to feel how passive the polyclinic in Japan is. In addition, New Orleans is a city where many Black people live, and the doctors and students were mostly white, but the patients were mostly Black. There was also a distinctive accent, and there were many scenes in which it was hard to communicate with them, but I interacted with people of a race I had never dealt with before and was able to deepen my knowledge and experience.

I think the good thing about studying abroad is confronting a new environment. How I adapt to and overcome that environment, and if I can feel my own growth in the process, that is the greatest joy. Through this study abroad I had many experiences I never had before. Although small, there were many times when I could feel growth. I want to keep working hard so that I can make use of this wonderful experience in my life from now on.

Finally, this study abroad could never have come about by myself alone. I express my heartfelt gratitude to everyone who supported me: the doctors of Nagoya University, the staff of the International Collaboration Office, the staff of the Academic Affairs Division, my seniors, my classmates, my family, and the people of Tulane University, who gave me such a valuable opportunity.
